meta.title: Ecru — your wardrobe, and the reason behind every outfit
meta.description: Ecru catalogues what you own, builds outfits from it, and remembers what you wore. Every time it says two things go together, it tells you why — in one sentence. No model, no cloud, no account. Free on the App Store.
hero.title: Your wardrobe, and the reason behind every outfit.
hero.lede: Ecru catalogues what you own, builds outfits from it, and remembers what you wore. Every time it says two things go together, it tells you why — in one sentence.
store.note: Ecru is on the App Store — free, for iPhone.
hero.fineprint: No account  ·  nothing uploaded  ·  every feature works in airplane mode
hero.alt: An item card in Ecru: the measured colour of a dress, and under “What to wear it with” two pairs scored 88 and 30, each with the reason spelled out beneath it.
trust.upload.dd: Your wardrobe lives in a database on your phone and is never sent anywhere.
trust.account.dd: No email, no password, no profile on a server.
trust.model.dd: Colour is arithmetic on pixels. That's the whole trick.
own.h: Lay it down. The app finds it.
own.lede: Ecru does not try to recognise your clothes. You lay a piece on anything plain that isn't its colour, and the app finds where the garment ends and measures the colour inside that edge.
own.p: You pick the category from a list, and that's the slow part: about a minute and a half an item — and exactly why nothing about your wardrobe leaves the phone.
own.fix.h: And when it gets the colour wrong, it says so
own.fix.p: A busy background, or a garment nearly the colour of the table, and the edge isn't there to find. Ecru doesn't quietly average the table into the answer — it says it can't see the edge, and hands you the eyedropper and the palette.
own.callout: The rules sit on the screen where you shoot — including the one that costs people their first attempt: a plain background only helps if it isn't the colour of the garment.
wardrobe.alt: Ecru's wardrobe grid: three columns of items, each with a dot showing its measured colour, and a counter reading 16 items.
wedge.h: Every other app hands you a number. Ecru hands you a reason.
wedge.score.note: A match score, and no way to find out what it noticed.
quote.reason1: “Both pieces are neutral — a combination that never lets you down.”
quote.reason2: “One tone, different lightness — a monochrome that doesn't blur together.”
quote.reason3: “Identical lightness — these two merge. Take a lighter top or a darker bottom.”
quote.reason4: “Different seasons — together you'll be either too warm or too cold.”
wedge.p: Every score is tappable, and every tap opens the reason for that particular pair. The score multiplies four parts — colour, occasion, season, pattern — so a weak part drags the whole thing down instead of being averaged away.
item.alt: An item card in Ecru showing the garment's measured colour, its formality, warmth and wear count, and its best pairs.
ask.h: Finished outfits, best first — or build one yourself.
outfits.alt: Generated outfits in Ecru, each a row of items with its own score, sorted best first.
ask.ask.p: Ecru goes through your wardrobe and returns finished outfits, best first. The one you like stays in My outfits, where you can find it any time.
builder.alt: Ecru's outfit builder, showing one row of candidate items per slot.
ask.build.p: Six slots: top, second top, bottom, shoes, outerwear, accessory.
calendar.h: “Wait — did I wear this already this week?”
calendar.lede: One tap on a piece — or on a whole outfit — writes the day into the log. The calendar gives you the month at a glance, the count for each piece sits on its card, and a wrong tap is one tap to undo.
calendar.alt: A month calendar in Ecru with a dot on every day something was worn, and the selected day's pieces listed underneath.
colortype.h: Twelve colour types, six questions, no draping appointment.
colortype.lede: Hair, eyes, skin, gold or silver, the veins on your wrist, how you burn. About a minute and a half, and one of twelve types at the end — with a palette and a list to avoid.
colortype.point1: It tells you how sure it is. A confidence figure, and the runner-up type when you sit on a border.
colortype.point2: You can overrule it. Pick your type by hand and the choice sticks.
colortype.point3: It never reorders your outfits. Harmony alone decides what comes first.
colortype.point4: Your own colours outrank it. Add a colour you always get compliments in and it joins your palette.
colortype.alt: Ecru's colour type result: the type name, its palette, the colours to avoid, and three axes from warm to cool, dark to light, muted to bright.
shop.eyebrow: 06 · When you're standing in a shop
shop.h: A garment in the shop, measured against the wardrobe you already own.
shop.lede: A piece in your hands, a queue for the fitting room, and one question. Photograph it, check the colour, answer three questions with buttons — and it compares the piece against the wardrobe you already have.
fitcolor.alt: Ecru's fitting-room chat showing the colour it measured from a shop garment and asking whether that looks right.
verdict.alt: The fitting-room verdict in Ecru, with the score and the best pairs from the wardrobe listed under it.
shop.note1.h: It won't tell you what you want to hear
shop.note1.p: The verdict averages the five best pairs, not the single best one. Any garment finds one lucky match.
shop.note2.p: To hear “take it”, at least three pairs have to reach good together.
shop.note3.h: Shop light lies, and it says so
shop.note3.p: It shows you the colour it read and asks whether that's right. Say no and you set it from the palette.
quote.verdict.yes: Take it. It'll fit right in.
manifesto.eyebrow: 07 · Why there is no AI in here
manifesto.h: No model and no server — which is why every score can explain itself.
manifesto.model.p1: Colour is an average over pixels. The score is a formula over colour, occasion, season and pattern. Nothing is recognised, nothing is trained on you.
manifesto.model.p2: This is why the app can explain itself. A neural network can offer you 92% and nothing more. Arithmetic can show its working.
manifesto.server.p1: No account, no sign-up, no sync, no cloud backup, no analytics. Your wardrobe, your photographs and your outfits live on your phone, and every feature works in airplane mode.
manifesto.server.p2: One honest exception: the app checks for its own updates when it starts. That is the only thing it downloads, and it sends nothing about you to ask.
manifesto.coda: The app simply never needed a network to do its job.
limits.lede: This belongs on the page as much as the rest.
shoot.alt: Ecru's capture screen: the rules for photographing a piece, the sheet-shade picker, and a “Take a photo” button.
limits.recognise.p: Category and pattern are chosen by you, from a list.
limits.fit.h: It won't judge cut, fit or size
limits.fit.p: Colour, pattern, occasion and season. Whether it suits your shape is still your call.
limits.backup.p: No cloud means no restore, and nothing to move to a new phone.
limits.first.p: Forty pieces is about an hour. It speeds up as you go — but we'd rather you knew now.
faq.h: The five questions people ask first.
faq.cost.a: Nothing. There is no subscription, no paid tier and nothing to unlock. With no accounts to keep and no wardrobes to store, there is very little to charge for.
faq.color.q: What if the photo lies about the colour?
faq.color.a: Then you tell it otherwise. Tap the item with the eyedropper, or pick the shade from the palette — and your answer sticks instead of being recalculated away. For pale neutrals the app asks first rather than guessing, because a warm bulb turns white into cream and grey into beige.
faq.move.q: Can I move my wardrobe to a new phone?
faq.move.a: Not today, and we would rather say so plainly than imply otherwise. Nothing syncs, and there is no export beyond saving individual photos to your gallery. It is the honest cost of keeping everything on the phone.
faq.suits.q: Why is “suits you” separate from the outfit score?
faq.suits.a: Because they answer different questions. Harmony is how pieces relate to each other; “suits you” is how a colour relates to your face. Blend them and neither can be explained.
faq.where.a: On the App Store, free, for iPhone. There is nothing to sign up for: install it and it opens straight onto your wardrobe — empty until you photograph the first piece.
finale.lede: Ecru is for making them usable again — quietly, on one phone, with its reasoning in the open.
